What is the gulf of execution?
where they try to figure out how it operates

What is the gulf of evaluation?
where they try to figure out what happened

What are the two parts to an action? 
Execution and Evaluation.

What are the three stages of execution?
Plan, Specify, Perform

What are the three stages of evaluation?
Perceive, Interpret, Compare

Stages of action (1). Goal
Plan the goal

Stages of action (2). Plan
The action

Stages of action (3). Specify
an action sequence

Stages of action (4). Perform
the action sequence

Stages of action (5). Perceive
The state of the world

Stages of action (6). Interpret
the perception

Stages of action (7). Compare
The Outcome with the goal.

All of the activity in the stages of action is conscious
False

How do radical ideas come about?
by reconsidering the goals, and always asking what the real goal is: what is called the root cause analysis

What is declarative memory?
memory for factual information

What is procedural memory?
memory that involves recalling activities

What are the three levels of processing within the brain, applicable to both cognitive and emotional processing?
visceral, behavioral, and reflective

What is the most basic level of processing?
Visceral Processing

Visceral Processing is referred to as the "Lizard Brain"?
True

What does the visceral system allow us to do?
respond quickly and subconsciously, without conscious awareness or control

The visceral system is tightly coupled to what system?
The motor system (musculature). This is what causes animals to fight or flee, or to relax.

Visceral responses are slow and completely conscious
False

For designers, the visceral response is about what?

immediate perception

Great designers use their aesthetic sensibilities to drive these visceral responses.
True

What is the behavioral level?
home of learned skills, triggered by situations that match the appropriate patterns.

What is the most critical aspect of the behavioral level for designers?
Every action is associated with an expectation

Behavioral states are learned
True

Expectations play an important role in our emotional lives.
This is why drivers tense when trying to get through an intersection before the light
turns red, or students become highly anxious before an exam.

What do behavioral states give rise to?
a feeling of control when there is good understanding and knowledge of results, and frustration
and anger when things do not go as planned,

Why is feedback important?
Feedback provides reassurance, even when it indicates a negative result

What does a lack of feedback create?
 The feeling of little or lack of control, which can be unsettling.

Feedback is critical to managing expectations, and good design provides this.
True

What is the reflective level?
home of conscious cognition

What happens in the reflective level?
deep understanding develops, where reasoning and conscious decision-making take place.

what is at work when a person is inappropriately accepting blame for the inability to work simple objects or attributing behavior to environment or personality
faulty conceptual model

What is learned helplessness?
The situation in which people experience repeated failure at a task. As a result, they decide that the task cannot be done, at least not by them: they are helpless.

Failure can be such a powerful learning tool that many designers take pride in their failures that happen while a product is still in development.
True

What is not failing a sign of?
that you are not trying hard enough

human error usually is a result of poor design
True

What is feedforward?
The information that helps answer questions of execution (doing)

What is feedback?
The information that aids in understanding what has happened

seven-stage model of the action
What do I want to accomplish?

Seven fundamental principles of design.
Discoverability, Feedback, Conceptual model, Affordances, Signifiers, Mappings, Constraints
DFCA - SMC

Principle of design(1): Discoverability
It is possible to determine what actions are possible and the current state of
the device.

Principle of design(2): Feedback
There is full and continuous information about the results of actions and the current
state of the product or service. After an action has been executed, it is easy to determine the
new state.

Principle of design(3): Conceptual model
The design projects all the information needed to create a good conceptual
model of the system, leading to understanding and a feeling of control. The conceptual
model enhances both discoverability and evaluation of results.

Principle of design(4): Affordances
The proper affordances exist to make the desired actions possible.

Principle of design(5): Signifiers
Effective use of signifiers ensures discoverability and that the feedback is well
communicated and intelligible.

Principle of design(6): Mappings
The relationship between controls and their actions follows the principles of good
mapping, enhanced as much as possible through spatial layout and temporal contiguity

Principle of design(7): Constraints
Providing physical, logical, semantic, and cultural constraints guides actions and
eases interpretation

When people use something, they face two gulfs:

FIGURE 2.1.The Gulfs of Execution and Evaluation. When people encounter a device, they face two gulfs: the Gulf of Execution, where they try to figure out how to use it, and the Gulf of Evaluation, where they try to figure out what state it is in and whether their actions got them to their
goal.
The seven stages of Action

FIGURE 2.2.The Seven Stages of the Action Cycle. Putting all the stages together yields the three
stages of execution (plan, specify, and perform), three stages of evaluation (perceive, interpret, and
compare), and, of course, the goal: seven stages in all.

The seven stages provide a guideline for developing new products or services. The gulfs are obvious places to start, for either gulf, whether of execution or evaluation, is an opportunity for product enhancement.

Harvard Business School marketing professor Theodore Levitt once
pointed out, “People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!” Levitt’s example of the drill implying that the goal is really a hole is only partially correct, however.

When people go to a store to buy a drill, that is not their real goal. But why would anyone want a quarter-inch hole? Clearly that is an intermediate goal. Perhaps they wanted to hang shelves on the wall. Levitt stopped too soon.

Once you realize that they don’t really want the drill, you realize that perhaps they don’t really want the hole, either: they want to install their bookshelves. Why not develop methods that don’t require holes? Or perhaps books that don’t require bookshelves. (Yes, I know: electronic books, e-books.)
Human Thought: Mostly Subconscious
Human Cognition And Emotion

FIGURE 2.3.Three Levels of Processing: Visceral, Behavioral, and Reflective. Visceral and behavioral levels are subconscious and the home of basic emotions. The reflective level is where conscious thought and decision-making reside, as well as the highest level of emotions

Flag - The Behavioral Level
Page 67

When we perform a well-learned action, all we have to do is think of the goal and the behavioral level handles all the details: the conscious mind has little or no awareness beyond creating the desire to act.
Reflection is cognitive, deep, and slow. It often occurs after the events have happened.

All three levels of processing work together to determine a person’s
cognitive and emotional state.

The behavioral level, which is the home of interaction, is also the home of all expectation-based
emotions, of hope and joy, frustration and anger. Understanding arises at a combination of the behavioral and reflective levels. Enjoyment requires all three.
The Seven Stages of Action and the Three Levels of Processing

FIGURE 2.4.Levels of Processing and the Stages of the Action Cycle. Visceral response is at the
lowest level: the control of simple muscles and sensing the state of the world and body. The
behavioral level is about expectations, so it is sensitive to the expectations of the action sequence and
then the interpretations of the feedback. The reflective level is a part of the goal- and plan-setting
activity as well as affected by the comparison of expectations with what has actually happened

Everyone forms stories (conceptual models) to explain what they have observed. In the absence of external information, people can let their imagination run free as long as the conceptual models they develop account for the facts as they perceive them.
It seems natural for people to blame their own misfortunes on the environment. It seems equally natural to blame other people’s misfortunes on their personalities

Flag 
Page 80

FIGURE 2.6.A Thermostat with an Explicit Conceptual Model. This thermostat, manufactured by
Nest Labs, helps people form a good conceptual model of its operation. Photo A shows the
thermostat. The background, blue, indicates that it is now cooling the home. The current temperature
is 75°F (24°C) and the target temperature is 72°F (22°C), which it expects to reach in 20 minutes.
Photo B shows its use of a smart phone to deliver a summary of its settings and the home’s energy
use. Both A and B combine to help the home dweller develop conceptual models of the thermostat
and the home’s energy consumption. (Photographs courtesy of Nest Labs, Inc.)
The Seven Stages of Action: Seven Fundamental Design Principles

FIGURE 2.7.The Seven Stages of Action as Design Aids. Each of the seven stages indicates a
place where the person using the system has a question. The seven questions pose seven design
themes. How should the design convey the information required to answer the user’s question?
Through appropriate constraint and mappings, signifiers and conceptual models, feedback and
visibility. The information that helps answer questions of execution (doing) is feedforward. The
information that aids in understanding what has happened is feedback.

Seven fundamental principles of design.
Discoverability, Feedback, Conceptual model, Affordances, Signifiers, Mappings, Constraints
DFCA - SMC

Principle of design(1): Discoverability
It is possible to determine what actions are possible and the current state of
the device.

Principle of design(2): Feedback
There is full and continuous information about the results of actions and the current
state of the product or service. After an action has been executed, it is easy to determine the
new state.

Principle of design(3): Conceptual model
The design projects all the information needed to create a good conceptual
model of the system, leading to understanding and a feeling of control. The conceptual
model enhances both discoverability and evaluation of results.

Principle of design(4): Affordances
The proper affordances exist to make the desired actions possible.

Principle of design(5): Signifiers
Effective use of signifiers ensures discoverability and that the feedback is well
communicated and intelligible.

Principle of design(6): Mappings
The relationship between controls and their actions follows the principles of good
mapping, enhanced as much as possible through spatial layout and temporal contiguity

Principle of design(7): Constraints
Providing physical, logical, semantic, and cultural constraints guides actions and
eases interpretation

The seven stages of Action

FIGURE 2.2.The Seven Stages of the Action Cycle. Putting all the stages together yields the three
stages of execution (plan, specify, and perform), three stages of evaluation (perceive, interpret, and
compare), and, of course, the goal: seven stages in all.

The seven stages provide a guideline for developing new products or services. The gulfs are obvious places to start, for either gulf, whether of execution or evaluation, is an opportunity for product enhancement.

Harvard Business School marketing professor Theodore Levitt once
pointed out, “People don’t want to buy a quarter-inch drill. They want a quarter-inch hole!” Levitt’s example of the drill implying that the goal is really a hole is only partially correct, however.

When people go to a store to buy a drill, that is not their real goal. But why would anyone want a quarter-inch hole? Clearly that is an intermediate goal. Perhaps they wanted to hang shelves on the wall. Levitt stopped too soon.

Once you realize that they don’t really want the drill, you realize that perhaps they don’t really want the hole, either: they want to install their bookshelves. Why not develop methods that don’t require holes? Or perhaps books that don’t require bookshelves. (Yes, I know: electronic books, e-books.)
